topStories.headline: With November Election Weeks Away, SoMa's 49% Sales-Tax Collapse Becomes the Defining Issue of the District 6 Race
topStories.dek: A stark data divide — SoMa revenues still near half their 2019 level while neighboring Mission Bay has grown — frames the contest between Supervisor Matt Dorsey and challenger Alex Behrend.
topStories.body:
The November 3 Board of Supervisors race for District 6 has sharpened around a striking economic reality: SoMa and Mission Bay, side-by-side neighborhoods in the same supervisorial district, are on sharply divergent post-pandemic trajectories. According to city controller data reported this week by Mission Local, SoMa generated roughly $9.4 million in sales-tax revenue in 2025 — down from about $18.5 million in 2019, a decline of approximately 49 percent. Inflation-adjusted figures for the first quarter of 2026 remained at roughly half the 2019 level, with little sign of a sustained rebound.

Mission Bay moved in the opposite direction over the same period, with sales-tax revenue rising more than 20 percent. The contrast, Mission Local found, reflects Mission Bay's new residential towers, the Mission Rock development, anchored tenants such as Visa, and a growing restaurant scene — while SoMa continues to be hollowed out by remote work, high crime rates, and persistent open-air drug use. According to 2025 police incident data, SoMa's crime rate was more than twice that of every other San Francisco neighborhood even as crime fell citywide.

Incumbent Supervisor Matt Dorsey, appointed to the seat in 2022 and seeking his first full elected term, frames the problem as one of public safety and police understaffing. His sole challenger, Alex Behrend — who recently qualified for Mission Local's candidate-coverage series after receiving endorsements from former Supervisor Dean Preston and activist Juanita More — argues the deeper issue is structural: high commercial rents and underfinanced local businesses. The two candidates have been answering a weekly question in Mission Local's "Meet the Candidates" series, with questions including how each would revitalize the Sixth Street corridor and hold homelessness nonprofits accountable.

District 6 covers SoMa, Mission Bay, Treasure Island, and Yerba Buena Island. Ranked-choice ballots will be mailed before the November 3 general election.

topStories.headline: Mission Bay's 398-Unit Affordable Housing Towers Get Building Permits, Clearing Path to Construction
topStories.dek: The city issued permits this week for both phases of Mission Bay Block 4 East — a 16-story and a 23-story tower along 3rd Street — bringing nearly 400 income-restricted apartments closer to reality.
topStories.body:
San Francisco issued building permits for both phases of the Mission Bay Block 4 East affordable housing development on October 5, according to reporting by SF YIMBY and Hoodline. The project, developed jointly by Curtis Development and Bayview Senior Services, will rise on a one-acre site along 3rd Street between Mission Rock Street and China Basin Street, directly across from the Third Street light rail line.

Phase one is a 16-story building at 506 China Basin Street with 165 apartments; phase two is planned to rise approximately 242 feet at 505 Mission Rock Street with 233 apartments, for a combined 398 units. The unit mix spans one- to four-bedroom homes and is priced to serve households earning 30 to 95 percent of area median income, including approximately 80 units set aside for families experiencing homelessness. Construction costs are estimated at just over $125 million across both phases. The project was granted a CEQA exemption under state affordable housing legislation.

Full build-out is expected to exceed half a million square feet of space, making it one of the largest 100-percent-affordable projects to advance in Mission Bay in years. A firm construction start date has not yet been announced, though the Commission on Community Investment and Infrastructure indicated last year that Phase 1 financing would be pursued in 2026 with a targeted construction start in 2027.

topStories.headline: Long-Stalled 'Lake SoMa' Site Has a Groundbreaking Target: New Renderings Show a 21-Story, 273-Unit Tower
topStories.dek: Updated designs and an estimated 2027 groundbreaking were published this week for 360 5th Street, the notorious water-filled excavation pit that sat abandoned for years between Clara and Shipley streets.
topStories.body:
Fresh renderings and a projected groundbreaking date emerged this week for 360 5th Street, the South of Market site neighbors long mocked as "Lake SoMa" after a prior developer abandoned a half-dug foundation in 2020, leaving it to fill with standing water. SF YIMBY reported on October 7 that developers DM Development and Thompson Builders have published updated designs for a 21-story, 273-unit residential tower and expect to break ground as early as next year.

The 249-foot structure would replace the vacant corner lot at 5th Street between Clara and Shipley streets, two blocks from the 5M development and four blocks from the Powell Street BART station. The revised proposal calls for 63 studios, 129 one-bedrooms, and 81 two-bedrooms, along with roughly 9,550 square feet of shared outdoor space split between a fourth-floor podium courtyard and a rooftop deck. Parking for 55 cars and 158 bicycles is included. Construction is estimated to cost approximately $68.95 million, not inclusive of all development costs.

Of the 273 units, 21 will be deed-restricted as affordable to households earning around half of the area median income. The project is leveraging the state density bonus to increase its permitted size. The original entitlement at the site dated to 2017; the current developer, Thompson Builders of Novato, took over after a 2024-filed lawsuit against the prior ownership. The project's website notes it is currently seeking planning approvals for the 21-story proposal.

moreNews.headline: Treasure Island's $222M Water Recycling Plant Nearing Completion as Commissioning Phase Approaches
moreNews.body: The San Francisco Public Utilities Commission's new Treasure Island Water Resource Recovery Facility is in the final stretch of a three-year construction effort, with an end-of-2026 completion target. According to the SFPUC project page, mechanical work is 90 percent complete, electrical work is 80 percent done, civil yard piping is 98 percent complete, and plumbing is 95 percent finished; startup and commissioning are projected to begin this winter. The $222 million facility, built by PCL Construction and designed by Stantec, will replace a 70-year-old plant and treat up to 3.9 million gallons of wastewater per day, recycling treated water for irrigation and toilet flushing on the island. The project won an Envision Platinum Award from the Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure in April 2025 — one of only two wastewater plants in California to earn that distinction.

moreNews.headline: SoMa West CBD Expands Community Safety Patrols Into Neighborhood Alleys
moreNews.body: The SoMa West Community Benefit District recently published a blog post describing an expansion of its community-based safety patrol program into the alleys of western SoMa, following the district's ongoing effort — active since October 2024 — to supplement city policing through uniformed Safety Ambassadors on bikes. The ambassadors operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, handling street disorder response, trespass enforcement, and referrals to social services. The alley expansion reflects continued concerns from property owners and residents that SFPD foot-beat staffing remains well below recommended levels in the district. The program is funded through special assessments on the approximately 2,765 parcels within the SoMa West CBD boundaries.
